en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Eighty,
Chapter on the Lesser Swans (Cūḷahaṁsavagga)
3. The Sudhābhojana Jātaka “I neither buy nor sell,
nor do I have any store of goods.”
"Truly, this small gift is of poor quality;
this handful of boiled rice is not enough for two.
"One should give even a little from what is little."
From what is middling, one should give what is middling;
from what is abundant, one should give what is abundant;
failing to give does not lead to rebirth.
This I say to you, Kosiya:
give gifts and enjoy them;
ascend the Noble Path.
One who eats alone does not obtain happiness.
His sacrifice is in vain,
and his striving is likewise in vain.
O Kosiya, I say this to you: he who eats his meal all alone while a guest is seated there.
Give gifts and enjoy them;
ascend the Noble Path,
for one who eats alone does not obtain happiness.
Truth has been offered by him,
and truth has been striven for,
by one who, when a guest is seated, [offers hospitality].
Someone else eats the food.
To you, Kosiya, I say this:
give gifts and eat yourself.
Having ascended the Noble Path,
one who eats but little attains happiness.
A person consumes their own past actions as fuel;
At Bahukā and at Gayā;
at Doṇa and at the ford of Timbaru,
in the swift-flowing great river.
In this case, one has offered a sacrifice,
and in this case, one has achieved one's purpose: when a guest is seated there.
Someone else eats the food.
To you, Kosiya, I say this:
give gifts and eat [yourself].
Having ascended the Noble Path,
one who eats not alone attains happiness;
for he swallows the hook.
The long thread with its binding:
he who, while a guest is seated,
eats his meal all alone.
I say this to you, Kosiya:
give gifts and enjoy them;
ascend the Noble Path.
One who eats alone does not obtain happiness.
“These brahmins indeed possess such magnificent appearance,
yet what is the reason for this dog of yours?”
"You transform yourself into various forms of diverse appearance;
tell us, O brahmins, who indeed are you?
"Both the moon and the sun have come here."
This, moreover, is Mātali, the charioteer of the gods;
I am Sakka, the lord of the thirty-three;
and this one is called Pañcasikha.
With hand-clapping, mridanga drums,
muraja drums, and alambara drums,
they awaken him with this music.
And having awakened, one rejoices—
those who are miserly and stingy,
revilers of recluses and brahmins.
Having cast off this very physical frame right here,
at the breaking up of the body, they go to hell— those who,
though seeking a happy destination, [act otherwise].
Established in the Dhamma, in self-restraint, and in sharing;
having laid down this physical body right here,
they go to a happy destination upon the dissolution of the body.
In former births you were our kinsman,
yet you were miserly, irascible, and evil-natured;
it is for your own sake that we have come here.
"Do not, being of evil character, go to hell!
"Surely you wish me well,
since you instruct me thus."
Thus shall I act accordingly,
doing all that has been spoken by those who wish me well.
This very day I shall desist.
I would not do any evil here, nor is there anything that I should not give,
nor do I drink water without having first offered it.
And as I give in this manner at all times,
O Vāsava, these riches will be exhausted;
therefore, Sakka, I shall go forth into homelessness.
Having abandoned sensual pleasures as they arise,
those best of gods, protected by the Lord, rejoice on Gandhamādana, the supreme mountain, the best of peaks.
Then the supreme seer, the protector of all the world, approached,
taking a branch from a most excellent tree that was in full bloom,
pure, fragrant, and honored by the Thirty-three gods.
This supreme flower, frequented by the best of the immortals,
was not obtained by mortals or by the *dānavas*,
but only by the gods who were worthy of it here.
Then four women, like golden palm trees—
the mistress of delights, Hope, Faith, and Glory, followed by Modesty— arose and approached the Sage.
Thus they spoke to the divine Brahmin Nārada:
"If this flower of the Pāricchattaka tree has not been assigned by you, O Great Sage, O Brahmā..."
"Grant us all our goals; may they be fulfilled for you as well.
May you also become like Vāsava to us.
Having observed those who were thus entreating him, Nārada—
Thus he spoke, inciting a quarrel:
"I have no need for any of these;
whoever among you is the wealthiest, let her wear them."
“O Nārada, having looked upon us as supreme,
bestow [this gift] upon whichever among us you desire;
for whomsoever among us you shall point out, O Nārada, [to him it shall belong].”
“She alone will be the one we regard as the most excellent.
“This speech is unseemly, O fair-limbed one;
what brahmin would incite a quarrel?”
"Go and ask the Lord of Beings himself;
if he does not know who here is superior or inferior.
Thus incited by Nārada, they—
Intoxicated by the pride of their own beauty,
they approached the presence of the Thousand-Eyed One and asked the Lord of Beings, "Which of us is more excellent?"
Seeing them, Purindada, the best of gods,
with his mind captivated, spoke thus with palms joined:
"O fair-limbed ones, may you all be equal."
“Who indeed, Bhadda, would raise a quarrel?
[She replied: “The Great Sage who transcends the entire world, established in the Dhamma, Nārada, whose conduct is truth.”
Thus he spoke on the excellent mountain Gandhamādana:
"Go and ask the Lord of Beings himself;
if you do not know who here is the highest and who is the lowest."
“That great sage, wandering in the vast forest,
does not eat his meal until he has received it on his noble hands;
Kosiya gives gifts only after careful discernment.”
"For she to whom he shall give it will indeed be better off.
"He who goes toward the southern direction,
along the bank of the Ganges on the slopes of the Himalayas,"
"O charioteer of the gods, bring the nectar to that Kosiya,
for whom food and drink are difficult to obtain.
Thus was Mātali dispatched by the Lord of the Devas.
Mounting a chariot yoked with a thousand [horses],
he approached the hermitage very swiftly;
remaining invisible, he gave sweet food to the Sage.
“Indeed, while I was attending to the sacred fire, Vāsava,
having overstepped all beings, [approached] the Light-Maker,
the supreme dispeller of the world’s darkness.”
Who indeed has placed in my hand this well-prepared conch-oil?
It is like a conch, white, of incomparable appearance,
pure, fragrant, lovely in form, and wonderful.
“Never before have I seen this with my own eyes;
O deity, what is this that you have washed so well in your hands?
“I have been sent by Mahinda, the Great Sage.”
The great sage hurriedly spoke with ambrosial words:
“Mātali, charioteer of the gods, you know me;
eat this supreme meal, do not refuse it.”
And when that food has been eaten, it destroys twelve evils:
hunger, thirst, discontent, fatigue,
sloth, anger, resentment, strife, and slander.
“Cold, heat, and hunger—this is the supreme taste.
“It is not fitting for me to eat, Mātali, without first giving; this is my supreme vow.”
"Nor does one who eats alone, who is unworthy of offerings,
and who does not share, find happiness.
Those who strike women and those who are adulterers— "
Those who steal from others and those who revile the virtuous—
all such people are base, with the miser as the fifth among them;
therefore, one should not even drink water without having given it away.
Whether for a woman or for a man,
I shall give a gift praised by the wise;
one who is faithful, generous, and free from stinginess in this world.
"These four maidens, esteemed for their purity and truth,
were sent by the Lord of Devas;
they are considered as such, resembling gold in their skin."
Hope, faith, and glory, followed by modesty,
came to that hermitage where Kosiya dwelt;
seeing them, everyone was filled with supreme joy.
"With beautiful complexions and crests like rows of birds,
four maidens from the four quarters," he said thus in the presence of Mātali.
“O goddess, who are you that shines in the eastern direction,
adorned like the most excellent star Osadhi?
I ask you, O you whose form is like a golden vine.”
"Tell me, which deity are you?
"I am the goddess Sirīhā, honored by men,
who always attends upon those beings who are free from evil."
"O one of supreme wisdom, we have come here because of a dispute over the nectar;
please distribute that nectar to me.
O Great Sage, give the nectar to whomsoever I desire."
Thus a man rejoices in all desires.
Know me as Śrī, O supreme sacrificer;
O one of excellent wisdom, share me with ambrosia.
“Men endowed with lineage, learning, conduct, and wisdom, and skilled in their own work—
those devoid of these find nothing at all.”
This which has been done by you is not good.
I see a man who is lazy and gluttonous,
even if he is of very noble birth and handsome in form.
Even one who possesses glory, noble birth, wealth, and happiness,
if he is guarded by her, sends [his followers] away like a slave;
she makes him serve every kind of untruth, associating with those who do not discern.
I know you are deluded, following after the ignorant;
one such as you does not deserve a seat or water, much less ambrosia.
Go away, for you are not pleasing to me.
“Who are you with white teeth, wearing earrings,
adorned with armlets and polished conch bracelets?
Clinging to a moist complexion, you shine forth.”
Having crushed the cluster of blossoms at the tip of the grass,
you look about like a doe startled by one who holds a bow and arrow,
as if you have been slighted.
“Who is your companion here, O lady with beautiful eyes,
that you do not fear being alone in this forest grove?
“I have no companion here, O Kosiya.”
O deity born from the essence of the *masakka* tree,
hope has come to you as a craving for nectar;
O one of excellent wisdom, share that nectar with me.
“Seeking wealth, merchants set out with hope;
having boarded their ship, they cross the great ocean.
Yet there they sometimes sink, and at other times they do not.”
Those who have lost their wealth come with ruined provisions.
Out of hope, farmers plow their fields and sow seeds, employing every possible means.
If, by this particle "iti," they do not rise up,
they obtain no fruit from that at all; instead,
they perform services for their patrons.
Placing hope before them, those men seeking happiness,
though they have exerted themselves for the sake of their master,
will again perish in all directions, having gained nothing at all.
Having abandoned grain, wealth, and kinsmen,
with hopes fixed on heaven and longing for happiness,
they perform even harsh austerities for a long time.
Those who have mounted a wrong path go to an evil destination.
These hopes are considered deceptive;
therefore, O Sudhāsaṃ, remove these hopes from within yourself.
“One such as you does not deserve a seat or water;
how could there be fine food? Go away, for you do not please me.
“Shining with glory, O glorious one,” she replied.
“O you who are called by the name Jighañña,
I ask you concerning this direction; O you with a body like refined gold,
tell me, which deity are you?”
“Queen Saddhā, honored by men,
who always attends upon those beings who are free from evil,
has come to your presence with a dispute over nectar.”
“O one of excellent wisdom, share that nectar with me. “Some people, at certain times,
take up generosity, self-control, liberality, and restraint,
and perform them out of faith.”
Some, once released from you, again commit theft, falsehood, fraud, and even slander;
such a man looks with longing upon wives who are his equals.
Even toward women endowed with virtue and devoted to their husbands,
and even toward women of noble family, he has restrained his desire;
yet he places his faith once more in Kumbhadāsī.
You alone, O Saddhā, are one who consorts with the wives of others;
you commit evil and neglect what is wholesome.
One such as you does not deserve a seat or water.
“Whence have you come, O nectar? You do not please me.
“She who is seen at night with her most excellent form and beauty vanishes when the dawn breaks;”
“O deity, you appear to me like that;
tell me, who are you, what kind of nymph are you?
You are like the dark clouds at the end of the summer heat, like a flame of fire.”
“Whose daughter are you, adorned with a garland of red lotuses, fanned by the breeze?
Why do you stand here gazing at the slow-moving deer,
speaking yet not releasing a word?”
“O Queen Hirā, honored by men,
who always attends upon those beings free from evil;
you have come here because of a dispute over nectar.”
"I am not able even to ask for food,
like a woman who begs while displaying her private parts.
"O fair-limbed one, you shall obtain it through righteousness and justice."
For this is the Dhamma, not mere begging for fine food;
even though you do not ask for it, I invite you to it.
Whatever fine food you desire, that I shall give to you.
Today you, O lady with a body like a golden vine,
have been invited by me to my own hermitage;
for you are to be honored by me with every kind of essence.
“Having honored him, even nectar would not be eaten.
Thus permitted by the radiant Kosiya,
Hiri entered that delightful grove where he dwelt.
The fruit, rich in moisture and honored by the noble ones,
is always frequented by beings free from evil.
Here, many trees have burst forth in full bloom.
The ambā, priyāla, and panasa trees, as well as the kiṃsuka;
the sobhañjana, lodhra, and also the padmaka;
the kekā, bhaṅga, and tilaka trees were all in full bloom.
Sāl trees, karerī, and many jambu trees here,
as well as assattha, nigrodha, madhuka,
and vetasa; uddālaka, pāṭali, and sinduvāraka trees.
The Mucalinda, Ketaka, and Hareṇuka flowers of pleasing fragrance;
the Veḷuka, Keṇu, and Tinduka;
as well as Sāmāka, Nīvāra, and Cīnaka grains.
The mocā, kadalī, and bahukettha plants,
the śāli rice, the pavīhaya, and the ābhūjina grains;
on its northern side—
A pleasant lotus pond has arisen;
it is not harsh, not overflowing,
and is fragrant with a sweet scent.
There the fish are delighted,
safe and well-fed;
the crocodiles are curved and crowded together.
The *satavaṅka* and the *rohitā*,
the *āḷiga*, *gaggara*, and *kākinnā*,
the *pāṭhīna* and the *kākamacchaka*.
There, the birds are fully contented,
secure, and well-fed:
the swans, the cranes, and the peacocks.
Cakravākas and kukkuhas,
many variegated kuṇālakas,
crested peacocks, and jīvajīvakas.
There, many diverse herds of animals come for drink:
lions, tigers, and wild boars.
Hyenas, brown bears, and raccoon dogs;
gavayas, wild oxen,
red deer, rohit deer, and ruru deer.
There are black antelopes and boars,
herds of wild pigs and sows;
there are many kadalī deer here.
There were cats with ears like hares;
the mountain-slopes were carpeted with variegated flowers,
resounded by the cries of birds, and frequented by flocks of birds.
Like a flash of lightning descending from a great cloud,
she approached, draped in blue garments like hanging branches;
her head was well-composed and adorned with a crown of kusa grass.
To one who was pure, fragrant, and clad in a deerskin, Hiri spoke these words to Atricca Koccha:
"Sit down, O auspicious lady; this seat is comfortable."
Then, while she was seated on a woolen rug, he—
wearing matted hair and an antelope skin— who wished to do so,
himself [offered] water along with fresh bowls.
The great sage, smiling with nectar, hurried forward.
She, having received it with both hands,
spoke thus with a joyful heart to the wearer of matted locks:
“Now that I have been honored by you,
O Brahmā, may I go to the third heaven as a victor.
Thus permitted by the radiant Kosiya, she departed.
Intoxicated by the pride of her beauty,
she approached the presence of the Thousand-Eyed One and said:
"O Vāsava, give me this nectar and victory."
Then Sakka also honored her, as did Indra and the gods,
that most excellent celestial maiden; with palms joined together,
she was worshipped by both gods and humans.
When he sat down upon the couch in the ninth [palace],
the thousand-eyed lord of the thirty-three gods spoke once again to Mātali, praising him.
“Having gone, speak these words to Kosiya:
‘O Kosiya, by what hope, faith, and glory,
and for what reason did you obtain pure modesty?’”
He brought forth that chariot, which was like a well-constructed vessel,
shining brilliantly like a benefactor,
resembling gold from the Jambu River and glowing like refined gold.
Adorned and resembling variegated gold,
many golden moons were cast upon it,
as were elephants, cattle, horses, monkeys, tigers, and leopards.
There the birds of the eṇeya species would leap;
there the deer were equipped with weapons made of beryl.
There the steeds of the king of horses were yoked.
A hundred thousand [maidens] resembling Susunāga,
adorned with golden nets and coverings, wearing wreaths,
possessing melodious voices, and unattached.
Having mounted that best of vehicles,
Mātali caused these quarters to resound—
the sky, the mountains, and the forest trees.
He caused the earth, together with its oceans, to tremble.
Having quickly approached the hermitage,
he stood with his robe arranged over one shoulder and his palms joined in reverence.
"Thus spoke Mātali to the divine brahmin: 'O Kosiya, listen to the word of Indra: [He is] one who is learned, aged, and disciplined.'"
“I am a messenger, Purindada asks you this:
‘Kosiya, for what reason do hope, faith, and glory consider hope as their food,
and why does modesty consider purity as its food?’”
“Fortune appears blind to me, Mātali;
for faith, O charioteer of the gods, is impermanent.
For hope is considered by me to be deceptive.”
"And moral shame is established in noble qualities.
"The young maidens who are protected by their family,
those who are aged, and those women who have husbands— [all these] I implore."
They restrain their own minds from the high-arisen desire and lust for men through a sense of shame,
as if at the head of a battle joined by arrows and spears.
When those who have been defeated fall and flee,
they turn back out of shame, even at the cost of their lives;
being possessed of shame, they receive them back again.
Just as the tide, with its oceanic force, restrains the waters,
so does shame restrain the evil person;
that shame is honored by all noble ones in the entire world.
“Indra, let that be known to you, O charioteer of the gods.
“Who has caused you to adopt this view, Kosiya?
Is it Brahmā, Mahinda, or Pajāpati?”
“Indeed, among the gods she was esteemed as the best;
as the daughter of Mahinda, she was born as a great queen.
Now, depart for the triple heaven.”
Having mounted this chariot which is mine to command,
O one of the same lineage as Indra, Indra himself awaits you;
go this very day to the companionship of Indra!
“Thus do those who perform no evil deeds become purified;
moreover, the fruit of what is well-performed does not perish.
Whosoever have seen the food of ambrosia, [they shall partake of it].”
They have all attained companionship with Indra.
You, Uppalavaṇṇā, are Modesty;
Kosiya is the monk who is a master of giving.
Anuruddha was Pañcasikha,
Ānanda was Mātali,
and Kassapa the Bhikkhu was Sūriya.
Moggallāna, you were Canda;
Sāriputta, you were Nārada;
and Vāsava was the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Sudhābhojana Jātaka, the third.
